Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/fortress-repo

# Working in the Fortress revival repository

The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**brief**
: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.

**original tree**
: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.

**record**
: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).

**walk**
: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.

**compiled path**
: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.

**component**
: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.

**api**
: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.

**area**
: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the run time), the library, or the specification.

**base**
: Commit that your work starts from.

**gate**
: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.

**harness**
: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.

**building**
: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.

**exploring**
: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.

You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.

## How a program runs

Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, run your test on both paths. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

### The phases

Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):

1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
2. Bind each name to its declaration.
3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
4. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
5. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
6. Mark each call of an overloaded name.

Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.

`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. Before the checker, it folds integer literals. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.

Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over comes when the checker accepts the interpreter's library.

### The compiled run time

`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:

- the component's functions, objects and traits;
- its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches

A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.

- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss":12:1~156:2 ...`.
- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.

In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).

`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.

### Parallelism and mutable state

Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.

`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A `value` object has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`.

Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:

- Most data is immutable.
- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").

So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.

Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`. The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

## The record

The record's main files:

- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.

Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.

## When to explore

Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:

- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.

When you switch, load `references/exploring.md`. It says which choices are yours and which go to the curator.

## Rules for every task

- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.
- Write the test before the fix for every edit of source code in the original tree. Add the test to the test suite and see it fail through the harness. Then make the fix and see the test pass. An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (`references/tests-writing.md`).
- Assert every value that matters inside the test, with the harness's own checks (`references/tests-writing.md`), and take the suite's pass or fail as the result. Do not compare the output of a whole run of tests with a saved copy, and do not add expected-output files. The gate's comparisons, and a comparison of outputs that your brief asks for, are the exceptions (`references/gate.md`, "Comparing with an earlier run").
- Take the tree that you start from as passing: its suites passed before it landed. Do not run them to check that. Start with your own failing test.
- Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate, a test or a measurement that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it. Run it again only after the code changes. Running a new program is not a repeat.
- Before you investigate a defect, or edit a file of the original tree, look for its rows in the gap ledger, with the queries of `references/records.md`, "Reading the record".
- After your fix, run your own tests. Run a whole suite where `references/tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite", asks for it, and nowhere else.
- Set up each Bash call as `references/build-and-caches.md` says, because every call starts a new shell.
- After an edit, take the step that `references/build-and-caches.md` gives for the kind of file that you edited.
- Run long commands (a build, a suite) in the background with a log under your tree's `tmp/`, and poll the log (`references/session.md`). Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing.
- Before you design a change to the library, study how the library already does the same kind of thing, and follow its way (`references/library.md`).
- Do not claim credit for the revival anywhere in a committed file. If git does not record who wrote something, reconstruct the authorship from the history. Do not guess it.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote. Do not commit scratch: logs, captured output, probe programs. Do not rename a file to get it past `.gitignore`. Each agent's transcript keeps how the work was done (`references/committing.md`).
- End your work with a report. List in it the defects that you found, your decisions, and the points that your brief asks for. Put a question for the curator in it as a decision not taken (`references/records.md`).

## The parts

Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words that you need to understand what the query prints.

The parts, in the order that work meets them:

- Setting up each call, building, the caches, what to rebuild after an edit: `references/build-and-caches.md`
- The Bash tool and its timeout, long commands and polling, waits and the prompt cache, stopping processes, interrupts and stops of the session's process, the automatic permission check: `references/session.md`
- The base and its build, worktrees seeded from it, the old code beside the new: `references/worktrees.md`
- The build failing, JDKs, scalac and ASM traps, generated sources: `references/toolchain.md`
- The interpreter area: walk's code (`interpreter/`), where a fix of walk belongs, its checks at load, its natives, running programs under walk, the microGPT check: `references/interpreter.md`
- The compiled area: the checker, the code generator, the run time, compiled runs, the `fortress` commands, the checker's time after a change: `references/compiler.md`
- The library area (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`): `references/library.md`
- The specification area (`Specification/`), Appendix I, citing it: `references/specification.md`
- What the revival changed in the team's Fortress, each change with its contradiction and reason; load it when a team source, an old note or your training disagrees with this skill: `references/revival-changes.md`
- Exploring: where to search, what to record and report, which choices are yours: `references/exploring.md`
- Writing a test: `.test` keys, `XXX` expected failures and their promotion, refusals at load, how a defect that you found is recorded: `references/tests-writing.md`
- Running one test, a few, or a whole suite, and when to run a whole suite; what runs outside the gate: `references/tests-running.md`
- The gate: what it runs and writes, the atomic runs, the ladder regression, comparing with an earlier run: `references/gate.md`
- Committing and pushing: `references/committing.md`
- What every report holds and where it goes, findings and points to report; POSITIONS, FACTS and the gap ledger; the queries of the record and when to run each; writing the ledger with `ledger.py`; the repository's history: `references/records.md`
- This cloud platform (the machine, the disk, the network, the platform's stops, the transcript backup, a lost container): the `cloud-container` skill.

A task usually needs several parts, and every task needs `records.md`, for its queries and its report. For example, a fix of walk needs `build-and-caches.md`, `session.md`, `worktrees.md`, `interpreter.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `tests-running.md` and `committing.md`. An edit of the library needs the same parts and `library.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

(*******************************************************************************
    Copyright 2008,2009, Oracle and/or its affiliates.
    All rights reserved.


    Use is subject to license terms.

    This distribution may include materials developed by third parties.

 ******************************************************************************)

native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$LineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Size")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$ToString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Size")

    uncheckedSubstring(r1: Range⟦ZZ32⟧) : String = do
    (* We could build a subString node here, but not until everything is working,
        because that will introduce
       SubString objects into code that may still expect FlatStrings.
       As written, this method always answers a FlatString.
       In any case, the FlatString object supports substring without copying*)
        assert((r1 ∩ self.bounds).isEmpty, r1.isEmpty,
                    "Empty substring of non-empty string")
        if r1.isEmpty then ""
        else self.javaSubstr(r1.left.get, r1.right.get + 1)    (* Java substr's endIndex is one past the last character *)
        end
    end

    opr =(self, other: FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Eq")
    opr <(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) < 0
    opr <=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≤ 0
    opr >(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) > 0
    opr >=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≥ 0
    opr CMP(self, other: FlatString): TotalComparison =  self.cmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CMP(self, other:String):TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CMP self)
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:FlatString): TotalComparison =
      self.cicmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:String): TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP self)

    (** get skips bounds checking. **)
    get(i:ZZ32): Char =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Index")
    cmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Cmp")
    cicmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$CICmp")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Substr")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32): String = javaSubstr(lo, self.size)
    javaIndexOf(c:Char): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$IndexOf")
    flatConcat(self, b:FlatString):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Concat")
    flatConcat(self, b:Char):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Concat")
    javaRegExpMatches(m:FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$javaRegExpMatches")
    javaRegExpSplit(m:FlatString, i:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$javaRegExpSplit")

    indexOf(c:Char): Maybe⟦ZZ32⟧ = do
        i = javaIndexOf(c)
        if i = -1 then Nothing⟦ZZ32⟧ else Just⟦ZZ32⟧(i) end
      end

    verify():() = do
        assert(self.depth, 0, self)
    end

    asDebugStringIndented(indent: ZZ32): String =
        spaces(indent) || "J" |self| "/" self.depth ":" self

    opr ∈(c:Char, self): Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ≠ -1

    rangeContains(r: Range⟦ZZ32⟧, c: Char):Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ∈ self.bounds[r]

    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
        concatenates **)
    opr ||(self, b:FlatString): String = do
        if b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
             (* Since both self and b have depth 0, balancing can't be necessary *)
            CatString(self, b)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end
      end

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
42	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
43	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
44	  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:
45	
46	         git push origin main
47	         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
48	         git push origin main:blinded-fable
49	
50	     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
51	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
52	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

23	## 4–9. The toy problem: histogram water
24	
25	Array of bar heights `2 6 3 5 2 8 1 4 2 2 5 3 5 7 4 1`; rain fills valleys; how
26	much water is retained? (Thanks to Dan Nussbaum and Steve Heller.) Key insight
27	(7–8): water level above each bar = `(max-to-the-left MIN max-to-the-right) − v`.
28	
29	Slide 9 — the concise Fortress solution, typeset only, its `∑` (blue), generator
30	(yellow) and body (green) highlighted:
31	
32	```
33	histogramWater(x: List⟦ℤ32⟧): ℤ32 =
34	               ∑                    ((left MIN right) − v)
35	                      →     ←
36	(v,left,right)←zip(x,MAX x,MAX x)
37	```
38	
39	(The arrows stand over the two `MAX`es: `x` is zipped with a left-to-right
40	running `MAX` and a right-to-left one. The deck gives no ASCII spelling of
41	either operator.) Notes: purely functional; allows map-reduce parallelism.
42	Pointer to Google Tech Talk "Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem" on YouTube.
43	
44	## 10–17. Principles
45	
46	- Slide 10 — **Three principles**: a growable language, a mathematical language,
47	  a parallel language. "We tried very hard to avoid including any language
48	  feature not clearly justified by one or more of these principles."
49	- Slide 11 — Growability: modular libraries (components and APIs, separate
50	  compilation, multiple co-existing implementations of one interface); break
51	  with Fortran's array emphasis — objects with *multiple inheritance* of traits
52	  ("Why inheritance? Sharing of code. Why multiple? Even more sharing of
53	  code."); distributed/hierarchical arrays; therefore *multimethods*
54	  (type-directed dispatch on multiple arguments).
55	- Slide 12 — Paradigmatic examples: extensible numeric hierarchy — multiple-size
56	  ints/floats incl. big, **"Rational, complex, and quaternion"**, interval
57	  arithmetic; vectors/matrices/tensors (matrix-vector both ways); collections;
58	  arrays (multidimensional, distributed, sparse). Goal: multiple implementations
59	  of the same interface coexisting in one program. **[repo]** Only rational
60	  shipped; this is the never-kept promise behind the §4d complex-numbers roadmap
61	  (seed: `complex_ring.fss` runs on the interpreter).
62	- Slide 13 — Operator overloading included: mathematical tradition; bad
63	  experience with Java's BigInteger/BigDecimal; contrast Gosling's C++ trauma.
64	- Slide 14 — Growability requires reliability: strong types; type AND method
65	  parameters may be types, operator names, integers, booleans, physical
66	  dimensions/units; design-by-contract (pre/post-conditions, inheritable
67	  invariants); rich library of algebraic traits (typeset only):
68	
69	  ```

73	  ```

75	  **[repo]** Spec-fiction: no operator-parameterized `Ring` ever shipped — the
76	  implementation has operator-fixed `AdditiveGroup`/`MultiplicativeRing`.
77	- Slide 15 — Algebraic traits, with the F-bounded self-type pattern and an
78	  `opr` parameter `⊙` (typeset only):

80	  ```

176	## 22–33. Syntax: whitespace, juxtaposition, precedence, comprehensions
177	
178	- Slides 23–26 — FORTRAN whitespace cautionary tale: `DO 20 I=1,125` (loop) vs
179	  `DO20I=1.125` (assignment to variable DO20I) vs `DO 20 I=1.125` (also an
180	  assignment!). Slide 26, the last build (23, 24 and 25 show its first two,
181	  four and six lines), its pairs labelled "DO loop", "also a DO loop",
182	  "assignment", "also an assignment!":
183	
184	  ```
185	       DO 20 I=1,125
186	  20   SUM = SUM + X(I)
187	
188	       DO20I=1,125
189	  20   SUM=SUM+X(I)
190	
191	       DO20I=1.125
192	  20   SUM=SUM+X(I)
193	
194	       DO 20 I=1.125
195	  20   SUM = SUM + X(I)
196	  ```
197	
198	- Slide 27 — Three uses of whitespace in Fortress: disambiguating vertical bars
199	  `{ |a| | a <- mylist, a | b }`; subscripting `a[i,j,k]` vs `a [i,j,k]`
200	  (reference then array constructor); *verifying intent of operator precedence*:
201	  `a+b·c+d` OK, `a + b·c + d` OK, `a+b · c+d` **rejected**. The code, ASCII:
202	
203	  ```
204	  { |a| | a <- mylist, a | b }
205	  a[i,j,k]
206	  a [i,j,k]
207	  a+b·c+d                 a + b · c + d
208	  a + b·c + d             a+b · c+d
209	  ```
210	
211	  The slide marks each of the last four OK except `a+b · c+d`, rejected. Its
212	  typeset twin of the first line reads `{ |a| | A ← mylist, a | b }`, with a
213	  capital `A` and the divides bar drawn taller; it renders `a[i,j,k]` as `a`
214	  subscripted `i,j,k` and the constructor as `[i, j, k]`.
215	- Slide 28 — **Juxtaposition is a user-defined overloaded operator** (function
216	  application and multiplication): `3 sin pi x - log x + 5 z^2 - 7 z + 2`;
217	  smart string concatenation `"I found" (n+1) "errors in" j "files"`; tight
218	  juxtaposition binds tighter than loose: `"I generated" n(n-1) "ordered
219	  pairs"`. Downside: operators must be distinguishable tokens (`MAX`, `MIN`
220	  uppercase). Scala contrast: any name infix/postfix, but no prefix operators
221	  beyond `+ - ! ~`. The code, ASCII (the first line Scala, the rest Fortress;
222	  the third is the "Compare:" line):
223	
224	  ```
225	  x = (item.x max item.y max item.z) min upperBound
226	  3 sin pi x - log x + 5 z^2 - 7 z + 2
227	  "I found " + (n+1) + " errors in " + j + " files"
228	  "I found" (n+1) "errors in" j "files"
229	  "I generated" n(n-1) "ordered pairs"
230	  x = (item.x MAX item.y MAX item.z) MIN upperBound
231	  ```
232	
233	  The polynomial's typeset twin, `3 sin π x − log x + 5 z² − 7 z + 2`, differs
234	  only in spelling. **[repo]** Verified empirically in the chat session:
235	  `opr juxtaposition` is real; `MultiplicativeRing` default wires jux→TIMES.
236	- Slide 29 — **Nontransitive operator precedence**: `a+b > c+d` OK; `p<0 ∨ p>9`
237	  OK; `a+b ∨ c+d` NOT OK — no precedence defined between + and ∨. "We use only
238	  the most obvious and familiar rules"; matters with hundreds of operator
239	  symbols; just parenthesize. The displayed lines, typeset only (the symbols,
240	  then the parenthesized forms):
241	
242	  ```
243	  ∪ ∩ ⊏ ÷ ⊕ ≼ ⊞ ⊗ ⋏ ⊚ ∈ ⋄ ⋆ ⋐ ⋖ ≈ ∥ ⊘ .
244	  (a + b) ∨ (c + d)    or    a + (b ∨ c) + d
245	  ```
246	
247	- Slide 30 — Binding `x = h+1` ("we see this on whiteboards!") vs mutable
248	  declaration `y:ZZ := h+1` (type required); assignment is `:=`; compound
249	  `y += 1`; goal: "mostly pure, SSA" style with a one-character tax. The code,
250	  typeset only:
251	
252	  ```
253	  x = h + 1
254	  y: ℤ := h + 1
255	  y := y + 1
256	  y += 1
257	  ```
258	
259	- Slide 31 — Comments support wiki syntax (superset of Wiki Creole 1.0);
260	  single backquotes embed Fortress code, rendered typeset. The code, ASCII
261	  (the slide's typewriter font draws the backquote as ‘):
262	
263	  ```
264	  //italic//  **boldface**  [[link]]  {{image}}
265	  (*) The **best** way to swap `x` and `y` is `(x,y) := (y,x)`
266	  ```
267	
268	  Rendered below it: "⊛ The best way to swap x and y is (x, y) := (y, x)",
269	  with "best" in bold and `x`, `y` and the swap in math type.
270	- Slide 32 — Comprehensions (Haskell notation) for arrays `[...]`, lists
271	  `<|...|>`, sets `{...}`, multisets `{|...|}` — with typeset equivalents.
272	  The code, ASCII:
273	
274	  ```
275	  [1,2,3]       [ |a| | a <- mylist, a | b ]
276	  <|1,2,3|>     <| |a| | a <- mylist, a | b |>
277	  {1,2,3}       { |a| | a <- mylist, a | b }
278	  {|1,2,3|}     {| |a| | a <- mylist, a | b |}
279	  ```
280	
281	  The typeset half has five rows, not four: `[1, 2, 3]`, `⟨1, 2, 3⟩`,
282	  `{1, 2, 3}`, `⦃1, 2, 3⦄` and also `⟅1, 2, 3⟆`, a second form for multisets,
283	  each beside its comprehension `|a| | a ← mylist, a | b` in the same brackets.
284	- Slide 33 — **Big reduction operators** = fold × comprehension. The code,
285	  ASCII:
286	
287	  ```
288	  BIG SUM [p <- mylist, prime p] p+1
289	  BIG MAX [k <- 1:n] a[k]
290	  BIG OPLUS [j <- 1:n, k <- j:n] f(j,k)
291	  ```
292	
293	  The typeset row below differs only in spelling: `∑`, `MAX` and `⨁` with
294	  their generators stacked beneath, `a[k]` as `a` subscripted `k`.
295	  "Reduction operators are exactly like comprehensions... Implementationally
296	  they are identical."
297	  **[repo]** `BIG //` / `BIG ||` used in mandelbrot_canonical.fss.
298	
299	## 34–37. Parallelism machinery
300	
301	- Slide 34 — The ∑ desugaring, all in library code (typeset only; a
302	  generator under a big operator is set on the line below it):
303	
304	  ```
305	   ∑   aᵢ xⁱ      MAX (aᵢ + bᵢ)     { (m, n) | m ← A, prime m, n ← B, m | n }
306	  i←0:9          i←0:9
307	
308	   ∑   aᵢ xⁱ  desugars to  ∑(0 : 9, fn i ⇒ aᵢ xⁱ)
309	  i←0:9
310	
311	  opr ∑⟦E, T extends Monoid⟦T, +⟧⟧(g: Generator⟦E⟧, body: E → T): T =
312	      g.generate(SumReduction⟦T⟧, body)
313	
314	  object SumReduction⟦T extends Monoid⟦T, +⟧⟧ extends Reduction⟦T⟧
315	      empty(): T = cast⟦T⟧ 0
316	      join(a: T, b: T): T = a + b
317	  end
318	  ```
319	
320	  "Definition of ∑ can be overloaded."
321	  **[repo]** `Monoid[\T,opr\]` DID ship — exactly enough for ∑ (chat-session
322	  audit).
323	- Slide 35 — Generators/reducers generic in element type; lazily composable
324	  (cross product, catenation); algebraic properties encoded in the type system;
325	  generator controls sequential/parallel strategy; overload dispatch selects
326	  best reducer per generator; **all defined by library code, not the compiler**.
327	- Slide 36 — Low-level cooperative parallelism: tuples, arguments, binary
328	  operators are the real basis, shown by slide 18's recursive line (typeset):
329	
330	  ```
331	  walk(x.a, left, x.b.val MAX right) + walk(x.b, left MAX x.a.val, right)
332	  ```
333	
334	  The compiler decides which subexpressions become microtasks (research area);
335	  work-stealing load balancing; "Goal: do for processors what GC does for
336	  memory."
337	- Slide 37 — Competitive parallelism: global shared memory; `atomic do ... end`
338	  appears to execute all at once, implemented with transactional memory;
339	  nesting with exceptions is "interesting".
340	
341	## 38–44. The type system, and where it broke
342	
343	- Slide 38 — Hand-drawn hierarchy: Any → {String, Boolean, Number}; Number →
344	  {Integral → ZZ32, ZZ64, ZZ; Float → RR32, RR64}. Will overloading work with
345	  `print(x: ...)` for each? The code, typeset only:
346	
347	  ```
348	  print(x: String) = …                 print(x: ℤ) = …
349	  print(x: Boolean) = …                print(x: ℝ32) = …
350	  print(x: ℤ32) = …                    print(x: ℝ64) = …
351	  print(x: ℤ64) = …
352	  ```
353	
354	- Slide 39 — How to say you DON'T want sharing (needed for the meet rule /
355	  overload safety): `excludes` clauses — **quadratic blow-up!** The code,
356	  typeset only:
357	
358	  ```
359	  trait String extends { Any } … end
360	  trait Boolean extends { Any } excludes { String } … end
361	  trait Number extends { Any } excludes { String, Boolean } … end
362	  ```
363	
364	- Slide 40 — Fix: `partitioned trait Primitive extends {Any}` — children of a
365	  partitioned trait are pairwise disjoint; hierarchy becomes Any → Primitive →
366	  {String, Boolean, Number(partitioned)}. The code, typeset only:
367	
368	  ```
369	  partitioned trait Primitive extends { Any } end
370	  trait String extends { Primitive } … end
371	  trait Boolean extends { Primitive } … end
372	  partitioned trait Number extends { Primitive } … end
373	  ```
374	
375	  **[repo]** `partitioned` never shipped; the implementation uses
376	  `comprises` + `excludes` (numeric lattice
377	  ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: QQ <: RR64 extracted from source in the chat session;
378	  `Number comprises {RR64}` seals the tower).
379	- Slide 41 — Fully symmetric dynamic multimethod dispatch on run-time types of
380	  ALL arguments (no visitor pattern); types never erased: dispatch can tell
381	  `List[\Boolean\]` from `List[\String\]`, both more specific than `List[\T\]`.
382	  The code, typeset only:
383	
384	  ```
385	  crunch(x: List⟦Boolean⟧) = …
386	  crunch(x: List⟦String⟧) = …
387	  crunch⟦T⟧(x: List⟦T⟧) = …
388	  myList: List⟦Object⟧ = …
389	  crunch(myList)
390	  ```
391	
392	  "… could end up invoking any of the three definitions".
393	- Slide 42 — Run-time type inference: `crunch(myList)` where
394	  `myList: List[\Object\] =` a list of threads must infer `T = Thread` at run
395	  time. The code, typeset only:
396	
397	  ```
398	  crunch(x: List⟦Boolean⟧) = …
399	  crunch(x: List⟦String⟧) = …
400	  crunch⟦T⟧(x: List⟦T⟧) = …
401	  myList: List⟦Object⟧ = a list of threads
402	  crunch(myList)
403	  ```
404	
405	  "needs to infer at run time that T = Thread".
406	- Slide 43 — Static parameters with interdependent bounds (typeset only):
407	
408	  ```
409	  mangle⟦M extends { PartialOrder⟦M⟧, Group⟦M, +⟧ },
410	         F extends M → N,
411	         N extends List⟦M⟧⟧
412	       (x: M, f: F): N = …
413	  ```
414	
415	  "In general, this requires solving a system of type inequalities at run
416	  time."
417	- Slide 44 — **Where We Got Stuck**: generic methods × symmetry requirement →
418	  parametric meet rule and return type rule → nontrivial run-time constraint
419	  solving — "'Non-trivial' is a euphemism for 'exponential cost'";
420	  "Contravariance and union types interact badly"; mitigated by imposing a
421	  lexical asymmetry on method type parameters; "another nasty case popped up:
422	  the return type rule has nontrivial consequences." **"So we had a grand
423	  vision, but could not quite pull it off."**
424	  **[repo]** This is precisely the subject of the trunk's final commits —
425	  karl.naden's `Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/` (incl. "rtr algorithm",
426	  "using constraints", RTRinstantionTheory.tex) and
427	  `Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`, preserved in the graft.
428	  [Correction 2026-09-23: these files are in the java.net trunk tip `a874948ac` itself (`justificationOfRTR.tex` from `8015b17f4`, 2012-08-31), not preserved by the graft; see `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.]
429	
430	## 45–50. Lessons and reflections
431	
432	- Slide 45 — **We learned some good things**: generic types with multiple
433	  inheritance of generic methods and symmetric dispatch; parallelism with
434	  automatic work-stealing; factoring parallelism on collections via generators
435	  and reducers; parsing AND pretty-printing mathematical syntax; nontransitive
436	  precedence; physical dimensions/units inside a generic type system. "My
437	  current thinking is to back off and try to exploit a subset of these ideas
438	  using a less complex type system."
439	- Slide 46 — Syntax tradeoffs: math notation designed for concision, not
440	  robustness; juxtaposition made programmable — "sometimes this worked
441	  beautifully, sometimes it required some weird contortions"; Haskell and Scala
442	  each capture a PART of mathematical tradition more consistently.
443	- Slide 47 — Reflections: **"I knew when I started the Fortress project in
444	  2003..."** (confirms the 2003 start; git history begins 2007-01-04,
445	  mid-project). Long shot vs Fortran/Java; "we are too often fearful of
446	  correcting mistakes"; JavaScript aside ("maybe Worse Is Better").
447	- Slide 48 — Language life cycles: good ideas survive by hopping between
448	  languages; "the language that develops an idea may not be the one that
449	  survives"; "I believe in studying history." Fortress → **Swift optional
450	  binding**. The code, typeset only:
451	
452	  ```
453	  if x ← z then f(x) else y end
454	  ```
455	
456	  "where the type of z is Maybe⟦T⟧".
457	- Slides 49–50 — Closer: Greenspun's Tenth Rule; slide 50 adds "a modern
458	  variation": any sufficiently complicated parallel program contains "an ad
459	  hoc, informally-specified, bug-ridden, slow implementation of . . . what?";
460	  "We need to figure out what 'what' is."
461	
462	## Code for a histogram-water demo
463	
464	The deck gives two of the four solutions of the talk "Four Solutions to a
465	Trivial Problem", described from its captions in
466	`research/extracts/SteeleGoogleTechTalk2015-extract.md` (line numbers below
467	are of that file). The input is slides 4–8's `2 6 3 5 2 8 1 4 2 2 5 3 5 7 4 1`;
468	the deck states no answer, the captions extract gives 35 (line 74).
469	
470	- **Slide 9 — the big-operator one-liner**: the talk's Solution 4, parallel
471	  prefix (lines 157–176; lines 166–167 identify it with slide 9). Beyond the
472	  deck it needs:
473	  - the two arrowed `MAX` operators over a `List⟦ℤ32⟧`, a left-to-right and a
474	    right-to-left running `MAX`, which the talk puts in the library as
475	    operators whose implementation it leaves open (lines 159–163); the deck
476	    gives neither a definition nor an ASCII spelling. **[repo]** The library
477	    has no running `MAX`; the nearest are `PREFIX_SUM` and `SUFFIX_SUM`, on
478	    `Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]` only (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2686–2687`);
479	  - a three-argument `zip(x, y, z)` that generates triples. **[repo]** The
480	    library's `zip` takes one other list, as a dotted method, `l.zip(other)`
481	    (`Library/PureList.fsi:75`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1332`).
482	- **Slides 18–19 — the recursive walk over a tree**: the talk's Solution 3, the
483	  monoid-cached tree (lines 135–155), as one downward pass carrying both the
484	  maximum to the left and the maximum to the right, the "careful coding [that]
485	  computes both at once" (lines 149–152); slide 36 repeats its recursive line.
486	  The talk's code names this sweep `process`, not `walk` (lines 342–343).
487	  Beyond the deck it needs:
488	  - `maxCachedTree`, which builds the tree from the list, each node caching the
489	    `MAX` of its leaves (lines 137–144);
490	  - `Pair`, with children `a` and `b` and the cached maximum `val`, and `Leaf`,
491	    with the bar height `val`;
492	  - a type that holds both `Pair` and `Leaf`, for `maxCachedTree`'s result and
493	    for `a` and `b`, so that `walk`'s two overloads cover it; in the talk this
494	    is `trait CachedTree comprises {NullNode, SingletonNode, PairNode}` (lines
495	    140–141);
496	  - a case for the empty list, which `walk` lacks; the talk's `NullNode` holds
497	    `MAX`'s identity, −∞ (lines 141–142).
498	
499	  These slides type the list `List⟦ℤ⟧` (`List[\ZZ\]`), slide 9 `List⟦ℤ32⟧`.
500	- Solutions 1 (three sequential sweeps, lines 80–96) and 2 (bitonic globs,

1	# Extract: Guy L. Steele Jr., "Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem" (Google TechTalks 2015)
2	
3	> **DRAFT — captions-only extract.** This is based solely on the human-made
4	> YouTube captions of the talk. The slides — full of charts, diagrams, and
5	> Fortress code in mathematical notation — were **not** available (no slide
6	> PDF has been found on the open web; see `research/README.md` for the
7	> recovery routes), so all slide content described below is inferred from
8	> what Steele says. Obvious transcription artifacts in the captions
9	> (garbled notation, lowercased "Fortress", split-up words) have been
10	> corrected in the quotations below; paraphrase stays outside quotation
11	> marks. A proper transcript aligned with reconstructed slides (frame
12	> extraction from the video) is planned, will be cleaned the same way,
13	> and will supersede this draft.
14	
15	- **Title:** Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem
16	- **Speaker:** Guy L. Steele Jr. (Oracle Labs)
17	- **Venue:** Google TechTalks (talk given at a Google office; introduced by "Matt")
18	- **Date given:** 2015-12-01; **uploaded to YouTube:** 2016-01-28
19	- **Duration:** 1:01:47
20	- **Video:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ftcIcn8AmSY
21	
22	Extract made 2026-08-22 from the full captions. Timestamps are approximate
23	(caption cue times). Cross-references to the palimondo/fortress repo state
24	are marked **[repo]**. This is one of Steele's two retrospective-era talks;
25	the other is the JuliaCon 2016 keynote (`SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md`),
26	whose slides 4–9 reproduce this talk's toy problem and cite this talk by
27	name. Where JuliaCon compresses the parallelism story to a few slides, this
28	talk develops it for a full hour.
29	
30	## Thesis [0:55–2:25]
31	
32	"The best way to write parallel applications is, as much as possible, not to
33	have to think about the parallelism" [1:10]. The real issue is
34	*independence of computation*, which today's languages can't express. His
35	"over-simplified slogan" [1:51]: "accumulators are bad. Divide and conquer
36	is good." And: algebraic properties are important — programmers should be
37	aware of them and communicate them to the compiler. This is the same thesis
38	as his ICFP 2009 keynote "foldl and foldr Considered Slightly Harmful" and
39	Strange Loop 2010 "How to Think about Parallel Programming: Not!" (both in
40	the adjacent canon list in `research/README.md`), here developed with a
41	worked four-solution example.
42	
43	## Warm-up 1: summing a million numbers [2:25–5:30]
44	
45	A Fortran DO loop summing an array (he first "forgets" to initialize SUM —
46	"a very common bug"). The loop's semantics are inherently sequential: its
47	computation tree has a long left-linear spine. "Fran Allen won a Turing
48	Award for devoting her life to writing compilers that can undo code like
49	this, and turn it into code that a parallel computer can really run"
50	[2:47]. A mathematician instead writes Σ — like Fortran 90's SUM intrinsic,
51	it "says what to do... but doesn't tell you how, so there's no commitment
52	yet as to strategy" [3:14]. Marking the DO parallel gives race conditions;
53	adding atomic makes it correct but sequential again. What you want is the
54	balanced pairwise tree: log-depth given enough processors.
55	
56	## Warm-up 2: length of a Lisp list [5:30–8:30]
57	
58	Linear-linked lists force a linear algorithm: "data can dictate the way code
59	works", and linearly-linked lists are "inherently sequential" [6:40].
60	Analogy to Peano arithmetic vs. binary numbers [6:48]: unary representation
61	is the list; positional binary gives log-size representation and (with carry
62	look-ahead) log-log addition. Then Haskell code for list length with a
63	*three-way* decomposition — empty / singleton / concatenation of two parts
64	`a ++ b` — where the code does not say *how* to split; if splits are
65	balanced and cheap, delay is Θ(log n). Multiway decomposition is the key
66	paradigm shift.
67	
68	## The trivial problem [8:30–11:15]
69	
70	An array of integers read as a bar chart; pour water over it; how much water
71	is retained? Credited to Dan Nussbaum and Steve Heller [8:39] (same credit
72	as JuliaCon slide 4); "it actually may have appeared in some Google
73	questionnaires for employment — I'm not sure" [8:41]. The example array
74	(height-16, answer 35) matches the JuliaCon deck's
75	`2 6 3 5 2 8 1 4 2 2 5 3 5 7 4 1`. Key insight: water above each bar =
76	(max to the left MIN max to the right) − bar height, so the per-bar
77	computations are independent — "this gives us a decomposition into
78	independent pieces" [9:25].
79	
80	## Solution 1: sequential sweeps (Fortress) [11:15–13:45]
81	
82	Audience-participation reveal that the code on screen is Fortress: "Fortress
83	is a programming language designed to look kind of like mathematical
84	pseudocode and to use mathematical notation. But I assure you this is
85	actually actual, functioning, running code, or at least it was as of three
86	years ago, last time I checked it" [11:40–11:50]. **[repo]** December 2015
87	minus three years ≈ late 2012 — i.e. Steele last ran Fortress right around
88	the July 2012 wind-down announcement and this repo's HEAD (Aug 2012). The
89	revival's green suite makes his code runnable again.
90	
91	The function `histogramWater(x)` does three loops: a left-to-right MAX
92	accumulation, a right-to-left MAX accumulation, and a final
93	MIN/subtract/accumulate pass. "I said the nasty word accumulation. This is
94	going to be a sequential algorithm" [10:14]. An optimizing compiler could
95	fuse the last two loops into a two-pass version — "that's a difficult thing
96	for a compiler to do" [13:15].
97	
98	## Solution 2: pure divide-and-conquer — bitonic globs [13:45–23:35]
99	
100	Recursively split the bar chart, solve halves, merge. The merge abstraction
101	is a "glob": a *bitonic* outline ("it can go up and then it can go down —
102	or, as they said of the Monty Python brontosaurus..." [15:10]) plus the
103	amount of water already inside (just an integer — the shape of the water is
104	never needed). Representation: list of plateaus (height–width pairs) left of
105	the peak, the peak's height and width, plateaus right of the peak, and the
106	water count — five components. Combining two globs has three cases (left
107	peak higher / right higher / equal); the awkward part is a three-way *split*
108	of one outline at a given height.
109	
110	The Fortress code declares `object GlobReduction extends
111	MonoidReduction[\Glob\]` [18:42] — "that's essentially a promise that the ⊕ operator, the
112	combining operator, is going to be associative. That, in turn, will justify
113	a parallel implementation" [18:45]. Is the complicated ⊕ actually
114	associative? He has verified it by hand ("It's a pain. It'd be nice to have
115	a theorem prover do it, or a theorem prover built into a compiler — even
116	better" [21:25]) — the same theorem-prover wish as JuliaCon slide 15's
117	`property` laws. **[repo]** `trait Monoid[\T, opr OPLUS\]`
118	(`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2823`) and `trait MonoidReduction`
119	(`:2952`, also `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss:414`) are exactly this shipped
120	machinery; the `BIG` operator desugaring lives in `__bigOperatorSugar` /
121	`__bigOperator` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1114`).
122	
123	Given ⊕, the solution is a one-liner [22:40–23:07]: map every element to a
124	singleton glob, hit it with big ⊕, extract the water component. "It was
125	very, very clever to be able to write this solution as a one-liner, once we
126	built up this very complicated data structure and its associated operations"
127	[23:10] — the irony is intentional.
128	
129	In Q&A [55:40–56:55] he concedes the glob merge is not constant-time: the
130	three-way split is a binary (log-time) decomposition of the outline list,
131	so combining is not O(1) and the overall delay is "probably the square of
132	log n". "I'd love to find a way to do better in this
133	approach."
134	
135	## Solution 3: monoid-cached tree [23:35–29:15]
136	
137	Build an explicit in-memory tree over the array whose internal nodes cache
138	the MAX of their leaves — a "monoid-cached tree", monoid being "a technical
139	mathematician's term that just means the operation is associative, and that
140	it has an identity" [23:58]. Fortress code: `trait CachedTree comprises
141	{NullNode, SingletonNode, PairNode}`; the NullNode holds the identity (−∞
142	for MAX); construction splits the list into approximately equal pieces with
143	a comment "parallel recursion here" — "Fortress allows the two expressions
144	in a tuple expression to be computed independently" [25:35]. **[repo]**
145	This is the same `maxCachedTree`/`walk` code shown (against a sequential
146	Scala twin) on JuliaCon slides 18–19; implicit parallelism of tuples and of
147	binary-operator operands is JuliaCon slide 21/36.
148	
149	Then a downward sweep passes information left-child→right-child to compute
150	the left-to-right MAX sweep in log jumps; mirrored, the *same* tree serves
151	the right-to-left sweep ("the MAX-cached tree itself is symmetric" [27:00]);
152	careful coding computes both at once. Two pages of code instead of four or
153	five, no bespoke glob structure, "and it made use of an abstraction, the
154	monoid-cached tree, that might actually be useful in other settings"
155	[29:00] — the beginnings of a library routine.
156	
157	## Solution 4: parallel prefix — the true one-liner [29:15–33:20]
158	
159	The sweeps are parallel prefix operations (checkbook running-balance
160	metaphor [29:30]). Abstract them as library operators — MAX with a
161	left-arrow or right-arrow over it, "a conceptual left-to-right sweep. I'm
162	not going to see how it's implemented any more than I see how big sigma is
163	implemented" [30:50]. Then: "Once I have those operators in my library, no
164	more boilerplate. I have a true one-liner in Fortress here — and this works
165	in Fortress" [31:20]: zip x with its MAX-prefix and MAX-suffix, and for
166	each triple `(v, left, right)` sum up `(left MIN right) − v`. This is
167	exactly the concise solution typeset on JuliaCon slide 9. He names the
168	structure: "this is a generate step in the yellow, a mapping step... and a
169	reduce operation, the big sigma. So this is map-reducing math notation. And
170	I think this is actually a really good way to program, not only in the
171	large, but also in the small" [33:00] — a pointed remark at Google.
172	**[repo]** The Library really does ship `opr PREFIX_SUM` and `opr
173	SUFFIX_SUM` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4480`, `:4485`) — each marked
174	"`(*) For now, use a sequential implementation`": the interface-without-
175	commitment the talk advocates, with the parallel implementation left as
176	future work.
177	
178	## The argument: deferring the sequential/parallel decision [33:20–40:30]
179	
180	Is the one-liner sequential or parallel? Deliberately unanswered. Inlining
181	sequential implementations + loop fusion yields the efficient two-pass
182	sequential solution (he has done the transformation by hand — "this is
183	about the biggest program I can do it by hand on" [34:20]); inlining
184	parallel implementations + "deforestation, which I would describe as loop
185	fusion on trees" [34:55] yields the two-pass parallel solution of the
186	monoid-cached tree. "This is the main point of the talk... it's possible to
187	write solutions to problems that don't have a commitment as to whether to
188	be sequential or parallel" [35:10], with the decision automated at compile
189	time or run time.
190	
191	Accumulation vs. divide-and-conquer, structurally: the accumulator's update
192	operator has type (solution, input) → solution — *asymmetric*, so its
193	computation trees are forced linear; superb for one sequential processor
194	(historical aside [36:20]: CPU registers were called "accumulators" from
195	Hollerith card machines through the early '70s), and space-efficient. The
196	merge operator has type (solution, solution) → solution: "Just from its
197	type signature, you can tell it has the possibility to be associative in a
198	way that the accumulator combining operation does not. And its
199	associativity is the key to parallelism" [37:55]. Also: "identifying this
200	associative combining operator usually lends deeper insight into the
201	problem" [38:10] — he only saw the monoid-cached tree after first building
202	the glob machinery.
203	
204	The algebra glossary in programmer's terms [39:10–40:00]: associativity —
205	"the way you group them doesn't matter, and that is the key to
206	parallelism"; commutativity — order doesn't matter; idempotence —
207	duplicates don't matter (MAX yes, + no); identity — "this value doesn't
208	matter"; zero — "the other values don't matter. I'm the king, and I trump
209	everybody else." Such invariants give the implementation "wiggle room"
210	[40:12] — the freedom to use parallelism, or not, as resources dictate.
211	
212	## Manifesto, then engineering [40:30–45:15]
213	
214	"DO loops are so 1950s" [40:59]; linked lists likewise (Lisp, 1950s);
215	Java-style iterators "still so last millennium" — the iterator API "commits
216	you to a sequential processing paradigm. As soon as you say, well, first
217	let's set SUM to zero, you're already hosed" [41:20]. A C/Java for loop is
218	"probably the worst possible way to say map" [41:35]. This has changed his
219	own style even for sequential code — to the chorus of critics' voices in his
220	head (Pixar's "Inside Out" [42:33]) he adds: "are you sure you want an
221	accumulator? Maybe there's a better way to do this" [42:25].
222	
223	Parallel languages are typically "a well-known sequential language, and then
224	bolting on a couple of parallel features on the side. I think it's possible
225	to do better. **Fortress was an attempt to do that. I think we achieved
226	partial success, but I think more needs to be done**" [43:00–43:10] — the
227	talk's central retrospective verdict on the project. Mindset: don't split a
228	problem into "the first and the rest"; split into equal pieces and merge;
229	map inputs to singleton solutions and merge those ("that's usually
230	trickier" [43:40]).
231	
232	Then the backing-off [43:47]: "I have put forward a rather extreme
233	manifesto... And I'm going to back off slightly. In practice, engineering
234	needs to be done." Optimizations: special-case singleton leaves; branching
235	factors larger than 2 — he cites Clojure choosing 64-ary trees (Clojure's
236	tries are in fact 32-way): "I'm not sure that 64 is the ideal number, but I
237	know it's way better than two. It's also way better than 10 million"
238	[44:35]; self-balancing trees (red-black, finger trees);
239	parallel near the root, sequential at or near the leaves; arrays at the
240	leaves; dynamic choice between sequential processing and recursive
241	subdivision when iterating an integer range — "This is something we were
242	experimenting with in Fortress" [45:14]. **[repo]** That experiment is the
243	generator/reducer machinery of `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` and the
244	work-stealing runtime (now on stdlib ForkJoin after the jsr166y retirement
245	rung).
246	
247	## Conclusion: parallelism management as garbage collection [45:15–48:10]
248	
249	Linear-decomposition programs are "very hard to parallelize. I repeat,
250	someone won a Turing Award for writing compilers to do that. It shouldn't be
251	that hard" [45:28]. Programs organized around independence and
252	divide-and-conquer can run either way, "with the decisions being made
253	dynamically according to available resources" [45:50].
254	
255	The GC analogy (compare JuliaCon slide 36's "Goal: do for processors what GC
256	does for memory"): garbage collection also dates to the 1950s, was feared
257	for decades, went mainstream with Java; we accepted its overheads because
258	manual management "is so terribly hard" [46:40]. "I argue that the
259	management of parallelism is very much like garbage collection. It's the
260	automatic assignment of processors, rather than the automatic assignment of
261	storage. It's the automatic allocation of code to processors, rather than
262	data to memory" [46:55–47:08]. Overheads will look daunting, then shrink
263	without disappearing, as with GC. In a world of wildly varying and
264	heterogeneous processors (and memories): "I think this is our only hope for
265	true program portability, and not to have to keep rewriting code every five
266	years" [47:45].
267	
268	## Q&A [48:10–1:01:30] — the retrospective material
269	
270	- **Getting the ideas into existing languages** [48:30]: purely functional
271	  languages are one strategy for independence, "Haskell, I think, is the
272	  preeminent example"; "we see now map-and-reduce features that are being
273	  introduced into Java, for example, that were quite explicitly inspired by
274	  Haskell. And I know that the Java design group at Sun, and then Oracle,
275	  has kept an eye on the Haskell evolution for about the last 10-15 years"
276	  [49:04] (i.e. Java 8 streams/lambdas, from the JCP insider). But bolting
277	  on leaves the old idioms "tempting the programmers" — "The question is,
278	  how do you get old things to drop off?" [49:40]. Language evolution and
279	  decay may beat designing from scratch.
280	- **The odds he gave Fortress** [49:55]: it's really hard to get a
281	  full-blown language adopted if it's unfamiliar and new, he agrees — "**I
282	  gave Fortress only, at most, a 20% chance of becoming big and making it.
283	  And surprise, surprise, it is in the 80%. But I think we learned a few
284	  things from it.**"
285	- **The JuliaCon invitation, before the fact** [50:05]: he has "had some
286	  inquiries recently from a Julia users group wanting to... hear a talk
287	  about Fortress, hoping it can inform the evolution of Julia, which is a
288	  language that has gained more traction and is headed in this direction" —
289	  this is the genesis of the JuliaCon 2016 keynote, seven months before it
290	  was given. **[repo]** The two talks are a pair: this one is the
291	  parallelism lesson in depth; JuliaCon is the full design retrospective.
292	- **Complexity objection** [50:30]: a Googler notes the concise solution
293	  "took the better part of half an hour to explain... to a roomful of Google
294	  engineers". Steele's answer [51:15–54:45]: he hasn't *proved* it correct
295	  ("you flatter me"); unfamiliarity is an education problem — poll: ~15
296	  hands knew parallel prefix, all knew Σ; he wrote papers on parallel
297	  primitives in the '80s at Thinking Machines (Connection Machine)
298	  [52:40]; and the analogy is the structured-programming revolution — the
299	  1972 ACM national conference go-to debate, in which he took part as a
300	  student, with Bill Wulf (BLISS: systems programming without go-to)
301	  [53:25]. "It's a matter of figuring out what are the relevant
302	  primitives" and building community consensus; parallel primitives could
303	  cover "90% of the structuring of our code" as if-then-else/while did for
304	  sequential code [54:00]. "It's a grand vision. It's the result of
305	  synthesizing 40 years of experience" [54:21].
306	- **Grammars are left/right-recursive** [54:55]: only because parser
307	  generators emit sequential parsers; "If your parser generator were going
308	  to generate a parallel parser, you might write your grammars... in a
309	  different way. And I speak from experience. I've actually tried those
310	  experiments" [55:10].
311	- **A thank-you from the audience** [56:55]: "I have used a lot of the
312	  things that you have built over the years. And I just wanted to say
313	  thanks." — "Thank you. That means a lot to me that you found something
314	  useful."
315	- **Which languages carry the torch** [57:30]: "Julia and Haskell and
316	  Clojure are probably the most widely used languages that are
317	  intentionally exploring in these directions. I think such exploration
318	  could also be done in say, Scala. But the Scala community, I think, has
319	  not made a priority of investigating that dimension." On Python [58:10]:
320	  he'd be delighted, but the exploring fraction is small; Julia's community
321	  is small "but they are really pressing in this direction. And they're all
322	  more popular than Fortress, you know? So help me, Obi-Wan, you're my only
323	  hope" [58:29]. "I'm just going around talking to all kinds of
324	  communities, including you, hoping to find some interest. And maybe
325	  you'll take it in a direction I never thought of" [58:40].
326	- **Inertia of today's larger community** [58:50]: more inertia, but "less
327	  resistance today to new ideas" than the fractious 1960s–70s ("Fortran is
328	  good enough for us, thank you — or COBOL"); he sees "a lot less of the
329	  programming language, religion wars" [1:00:10].
330	- **UI programming** [1:00:20]: "part of the problem is that our users tend
331	  to be sequential. If only we had parallel users, then things might be
332	  easier" [1:00:53]; HTML designed differently would expose more
333	  independent parts of a page; "I think there's opportunity everywhere" —
334	  whether to exploit it is engineering.
335	
336	## Open items for the slide-aligned redo
337	
338	- Reconstruct the slides by frame extraction from the video (route 3 in
339	  `research/README.md`); align quotes to slide numbers as in the JuliaCon
340	  extract.
341	- Recover the exact Fortress code for: the three-loop sequential
342	  `histogramWater`, the glob object/⊕/split, the CachedTree +
343	  `process` two-pass sweep, and the prefix/suffix one-liner — then try to
344	  run them on the revived interpreter. **[repo]** JuliaCon slide 9 gives
345	  the one-liner's typeset form; the rest exists only in this video.
346	- Check whether the talk's deck is another Archivist DOC_ID on the Oracle
347	  Labs APEX host (CDX enumeration, `research/README.md`).
348

# Research: the Guy Steele Fortress corpus

Index of primary sources on the design and history of Fortress, maintained as
part of the revival effort. **Links and metadata only** — the documents
themselves are copyrighted (Oracle's notice permits personal/classroom copies
but not redistribution), so PDFs live in `decks/`, which is gitignored and
local-only: drop the files in manually each session; they are never committed.
`extracts/` holds committed working notes on the sources — our own summaries
and commentary with brief attributed quotations, never document reproductions,
except, at Pavol's word, the POPL 2019 paper (open access) and the checked
transcript of its talk with the slides' text.

## Talks and decks

- **JuliaCon 2016 keynote — "Fortress Features and Lessons Learned"**
  - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EZD3Scuv02g
  - Slides: originally on the Oracle Labs APEX document server as `DOC_ID:952`
    (host `labs.oracle.com` found dead/NXDOMAIN in 2026 checks; possibly
    intermittently back — a search index shows
    `https://labs.oracle.com/pls/apex/f?p=94065:10:2849938467431:5316`).
    Recovered from the Wayback Machine (identical digest across ~100 captures
    2021–2026); raw-bytes download:
    `https://web.archive.org/web/20260416152624id_/https://labs.oracle.com/pls/apex/f?p=LABS:0:100315543614648:APPLICATION_PROCESS=GETDOC_INLINE:::DOC_ID:952`
    (fallback, earliest capture:
    `https://web.archive.org/web/20211209023131id_/https://labs.oracle.com/pls/apex/f?p=LABS:0:101713034580486:APPLICATION_PROCESS=GETDOC_INLINE:::DOC_ID:952`)
  - Local copy: `decks/SteeleJuliaCon2016.pdf`; committed working extract:
    `extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md`.
  - Key slides: 9 (histogramWater ∑), 14 (`trait ℤ extends {Ring⟦ℤ,+,×⟧, …}`),
    15–16 (algebraic traits with `property` laws; BooleanAlgebra), 27–29
    (whitespace, juxtaposition, nontransitive precedence), 34 (∑ over Monoid),
    38–40 (hierarchy, excludes/partitioned), 44 (where the type system got
    stuck), 45 (lessons), 47 (project started 2003), 48 (Swift optional
    binding as a Fortress descendant).
  - The deck cites **Archivist 2012-0104 and 2012-0284** — presumably further
    DOC_IDs on the same APEX host; not yet recovered.

- **JAOO 2008 — "Fortress: programming for supercomputers"** — InfoQ, Jan 2008.

- **April 2005 Sun deck** (v1.02) — live mirror:
  https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/neal-glew/mcrt/Fortress/1.02_steele.pdf
  ("Asterisks are for accountants"; units as free-abelian-group metaclasses.)

- **Google Tech Talk — "Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem"** (cited on
  JuliaCon slide 9) — video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ftcIcn8AmSY
  (recorded 2015-12-01). **No slide PDF on the open web** (verified
  2026-08-18); as a 2015 Oracle Labs talk the deck is presumably another
  Archivist DOC_ID on the dead APEX host. Recovery routes:
  1. One-shot enumeration of every distinct archived Archivist PDF — each row
     is one recoverable document, DOC_ID in the URL:
     `https://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=labs.oracle.com/pls/apex/f*&filter=mimetype:application/pdf&collapse=digest&fl=timestamp,original,digest&limit=2000`
  2. Browse the archived publications app capture (the `p=94065` page) for the
     title, take its GETDOC link, prefix `web.archive.org/web/<timestamp>id_/`.
  3. Fallback if never crawled: the slides are full-frame in the video — frame
     extraction (local task). Note JuliaCon slides 4–9 already reproduce the
     talk's opening toy problem.

- Adjacent canon: ICFP 2009 foldl/foldr keynote; Strange Loop 2010 "How to
  Think about Parallel Programming: Not!"; "Growing a Language" (OOPSLA 1998).

## Papers

- **"Growing a Syntax"** — Eric Allen, Ryan Culpepper, Janus Dam Nielsen, Jon
  Rafkind, Sukyoung Ryu; Foundations of Object-Oriented Languages (FOOL), 24
  January 2009, Savannah, Georgia; 11 pages, © Sun Microsystems.
  - PDF: https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~aldrich/FOOL09/allen.pdf (the FOOL'09 program
    page at CMU still hosts the accepted papers).
  - Storage: the PDF is not committed (copyright Sun Microsystems, now Oracle, no redistribution granted), the same rule as for the Oracle decks; it lives in the ignored `research/decks/` per session and is reached by the link above. The Wayback Machine could not be reached from this container to capture the URL; a capture from another machine would make the link durable.
  - Local copy: `decks/GrowingASyntax-FOOL2009.pdf`; committed working extract:
    `extracts/growing-a-syntax.md`.
  - The design document for Fortress's syntactic abstraction (`grammar … end`):
    the spec's DSL chapter is a one-line stub deferring to this paper
    (`Specification/advanced/domain-specific-languages.tex`, `\cite{fool09}`), so
    this is the only prose specification of the mechanism the APL probes exercise.

- **"Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance"** — Gyunghee
  Park, Jaemin Hong, Guy L. Steele Jr., Sukyoung Ryu; Proc. ACM Program.
  Lang. 3, POPL, Article 11, January 2019, 28 pages; doi:10.1145/3290324.
  - Source: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290324; the PDF,
    https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3290324?download=true, was downloaded
    by Pavol on 2026-09-29 (28 pages, SHA-256
    `791f978e529b17d533e3342763ed6c54a2f1027eeee5aac9869956b5cdd2b954`). The
    copy the record read on 2026-09-23 was the Wayback capture
    http://web.archive.org/web/20240415191855/https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3290324.
  - License, as printed on the first page: "licensed under a Creative Commons
    Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. © 2019 Copyright held
    by the owner/author(s)." It permits non-commercial redistribution with
    attribution. On that license the curator made it the one exception to
    keeping copyrighted PDFs out of the repository.
  - Committed: the PDF, `extracts/ParkPOPL2019.pdf`, its full text from
    `pdftotext -layout`, `extracts/ParkPOPL2019.txt`, and the working extract,
    `extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`.
  - The talk: Gyunghee Park presented the paper at POPL 2019 on 17 January
    2019; video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eqpe-VfW3F4. Committed: its
    transcript, `extracts/ParkPOPL2019-talk.md`, made from the ACM video's
    audio by Whisper large-v3 and Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, their disagreements settled
    against the slides and the paper, with every slide of the speaker's
    Keynote deck written out as text; how it was made,
    `extracts/ParkPOPL2019-talk-pipeline.md`; the scripts and the two models'
    head-to-head, `tools/transcribe/`. The deck, attached to the talk page,
    and the audio are kept locally in `decks/popl2019-park-talk/`.
  - The type group's last published word on Fortress's type system. Its
    calculus FGFV keeps the exclusion rule as an ancestor rule
    ([Anc-Same-Trait]), adds declaration-site variance, and makes dispatch
    check the call's static return type, which picks the instance of the
    declaration the argument types select and never another declaration. It
    sketches a type soundness proof, with full proofs in a companion report.
    It has no self types, numeric tower, closed types or nominal exclusion.

## Recovery technique (Wayback CDX)

The APEX server serves documents by DOC_ID under per-session URLs, so filename
searches find nothing. Enumerate what the crawler touched with CDX:

    https://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=labs.oracle.com/pls/apex/f*&filter=original:.*GETDOC.*

Append `id_` after the capture timestamp in a Wayback URL to get raw bytes.
Note: Claude Code cloud containers currently cannot reach web.archive.org or
labs.oracle.com (network policy); the CDX/browser legwork has to happen on an
unrestricted machine.

## Open hunts

- Archivist 2012-0104 and 2012-0284 (see above).
- Pre-2007 project record: all GitHub mirrors' git history starts 2007-01-04,
  but the project began in 2003 (confirmed by JuliaCon slide 47). The earlier
  record lived on Sun-internal systems and java.net SVN (shut down 2017);
  survival of archives unverified.
- ~~Pre-1.0 spec drafts (2005–2007) with whimsical version numbers~~ CONFIRMED
  (2026-08-21): the PLRG publications page lists 0.618, 0.707, 0.785, 0.866,
  0.903, 0.954, 1.0α, 1.0β, and draft PDFs survive in the Wayback Machine —
  snapshot URLs and the whole recovered picture of the project websites
  (front-page pitch, wind-down post, community mechanics, verified captures):
  `extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md`.
- The 1.0 specification PDF (March 31, 2008 per its title page) as published —
  the richer working LaTeX (with editorial notes) is already in this repo under
  `Specification/` and `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; spec co-author Sam
  Tobin-Hochstadt hosts a byte-identical copy at
  https://samth.github.io/fortress-spec.pdf (SHA-256 verified 2026-08-21).
- Sun-era mailing-list archives (fortress-announce and the
  projectfortress.java.net lists) — no archive of the contents found anywhere
  (verified 2026-08-21; see the dead-ends list in the websites extract).

# Extract: the Fortress code of "Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem"

Working notes on the code slides of Guy L. Steele Jr.'s Google TechTalk
(2015-12-01, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ftcIcn8AmSY, slides (c) 2015
Oracle). Transcribed by hand from screenshots of the talk video (supplied
by Pavol, 2026-08-24) back to ASCII Fortress source -- the inverse of what
bin/fortick does. Our own transcription and commentary; per repo policy no
slide images are committed. Companion to
SteeleGoogleTechTalk2015-extract.md (the captions-only content extract,
which carries the timestamps).

## s1-sequential.jpg — "Sequential Code" (Solution 1)

```fortress
histogramWater(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): ZZ32 = do
  n = |x|
  if n = 0 then 0 else
    left = array[\ZZ32\](n)
    left[0] := x[0]
    for k <- seq(1 : n-1) do left[k] := left[k-1] MAX x[k] end
    right = array[\ZZ32\](n)
    right[n-1] := x[n-1]
    for k <- seq(n-2 : 0 : -1) do right[k] := right[k+1] MAX x[k] end
    result: ZZ32 := 0
    for k <- seq(0 : n-1) do result += ((left[k] MIN right[k]) - x[k]) end
    result
  end
end
```

Idioms: strided range `seq(n-2:0:-1)`; compound assignment `+=`;

Why?
• Good sequential code minimizes total number of operations.
  > Clever tricks to reuse previously computed results.
  > Good parallel code often performs redundant operations
    to reduce communication.
• Good sequential algorithms minimize space usage.
  > Clever tricks to reuse storage.
  > Good parallel code often requires extra space to permit
    temporal decoupling.
• Sequential idioms stress linear problem decomposition.
  > Process one thing at a time and accumulate results.
  > Good parallel code usually requires multiway problem
    decomposition and multiway aggregation of results.

For filter, unlike summation, we rely on maintaining
the original order of the elements in the input list.

Do not confuse the ordering of elements in the result list (which
